articles.title: Fork, Fix, Delete: Safe Database Migrations with GitHub Copilot and Tiger Cloud
articles.excerpt: What I Built A safe production workflow for fixing slow time-series queries without ever touching prod. The problem: Direct fixes on Postgres are risky. A bad index, a wrong type, or a long ALTER TABL…
articles.body: What I Built A safe production workflow for fixing slow time-series queries without ever touching prod. The problem: Direct fixes on Postgres are risky. A bad index, a wrong type, or a long ALTER TABLE can lock production. My solution: Fork / Fix / Delete using GitHub Copilot Agent Mode + Tiger Cloud MCP. FORK: Copilot called tiger_create_fork and cloned my live service db-63453 into db-63453-test (isolated, same data) FIX: Inside the fork, I reproduced the slow query. Used EXPLAIN ANALYZE , converted the table to a hypertable, fixed timestamp types to timestamptz , and added proper time-based indexes. Also used Tiger's Dump & Restore for migrating tables. DELETE: Verified with docs search via MCP, then ran tiger_delete_service — fork gone, prod untouched and still READY .

articles.title: Ubuntu / Kubuntu 26.04 — Prefer GNU coreutils
articles.excerpt: GNU coreutils or uutils coreutils? Ubuntu 26.04 ships with both. I prefer to use the GNU coreutils, for several reasons: The uutils are written in Rust and therefore make use of the Rust/Cargo modules…
articles.body: GNU coreutils or uutils coreutils? Ubuntu 26.04 ships with both. I prefer to use the GNU coreutils, for several reasons: The uutils are written in Rust and therefore make use of the Rust/Cargo modules. This is an ecosystem of small modules, each written by a different author and sometimes maintained, but more often unmaintained over longer time. This ecosystem is vulnerable to the same kinds of supply chain attacks as we have seen in the npm world, where packages are occasionally taken over by malicious people (either because the maintainer behaves in an irresponsible way, or by takeover via stolen credentials, or by domain name squatting, etc.). I cannot trust a package that relies on 100 or more such modules.

articles.excerpt: If Blue Origin goes public, it will have to meet the expectations of shareholders. Jeff Bezos may therefore want to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing.
articles.body: Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . Jeff Bezos , the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin , his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen.

articles.title: YouTube’s war on the Dislike button appears to be far from over
articles.excerpt: YouTube's new UI experiment is giving users plenty to dislike.
articles.body: TL;DR YouTube is testing a change that hides the dislike button on long-form videos inside the three-dot menu. The button hasn’t been removed entirely, but the extra step could discourage viewers from leaving negative feedback. The change appears limited to a small group of users, but a similar experiment on Shorts eventually led to the dislike button’s removal. YouTube is no stranger to controversial design changes , and if you thought that it was done messing with how dislikes work on the platform, think again. What started out as YouTube removing the dislike counter all the way back in 2021 matured into the streaming giant removing the button on the platform’s short-form videos. Now, it looks like the same treatment will make its way to the platform’s long-form videos.

articles.excerpt: And yes, it has AI.
articles.body: HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars. Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space. This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface.

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.excerpt: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tec…
articles.body: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

articles.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
articles.excerpt: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massi…
articles.body: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
